title: Slab-built wall letter monogram
subtitle: A large single letter in slab-built air-dry clay, 10-15 cm tall, for wall display
excerpt: A wall letter monogram is a single capital letter about 10-15 cm tall built from air-dry clay slabs and hung on a wall as a decorative piece or house sign. The letter is cut from a rolled slab, edged with a second slab strip for depth, and painted or left in the natural clay tone. No kiln is needed. Beginner makers who are comfortable cutting basic shapes can complete this project in one session.
sourceNotes: Slab-building method derived from first principles. Monogram lettering references drawn from V&A open-access collection (historical typographic and decorative arts).

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, the starting form for this project
The joining method: roughen both clay surfaces with a needle, apply clay slip, and press together firmly to form a permanent bond
The stage at which clay holds its shape firmly but is still damp enough to join, trim, and refine
Fully air-dried clay that is pale, lightweight, and ready for sealing or painting

content.text: A wall letter monogram is a single capital letter, 10-15 cm tall, cut from a rolled air-dry clay
slab

and given depth by a strip of slab clay around the edge, producing a three-dimensional letter that hangs on a wall. No kiln is needed. A beginner comfortable with cutting basic shapes can make this piece in one session, finishing with a painted or natural clay surface.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body, thinned with water)
Matte acrylic varnish or PVA diluted 50/50 (for sealing)
Picture-hanging adhesive strip or small hook and screw

content.text: Preparation

Print or draw the target letter at the correct finished size: 10-15 cm tall, in a bold typeface with no very thin strokes. Serif letters and bold san-serif fonts both work; delicate thin-stroke typefaces are fragile in clay and not suitable for a first attempt. Cut out the printed letter and use it as a template. Letters with enclosed counters (the inner hole of B, D, O, P, Q, R) require cutting out the interior: use the fettling knife carefully for these and work at leather-hard stage where the clay is firm enough not to close back up.
Building the letter
Roll a slab 7 mm thick, large enough to contain the letter template with at least 2 cm of space on all sides. Use guide strips on each side of the rolling pin to keep the thickness even.

Lay the paper letter template on the slab and hold it flat. Use the fettling knife to cut around the outline of the letter, holding the knife vertical for clean-edged cuts. Cut continuous strokes along straight edges; use the tip of the knife for curves, rotating the slab rather than the knife. Remove the template and lift away the waste clay from around the letter.

If the letter has enclosed counters (the holes in B, D, O, etc.), leave these uncut for now. The counter will be cut at leather-hard stage when the clay is firm enough to hold the shape without the inner waste piece supporting the walls.

Roll a second slab 6 mm thick for the edge strip. Cut a strip 1.5 cm wide and long enough to run around the entire perimeter of the letter. For a complex letter like B or K, you may need several pieces joined end to end with
score-and-slip
joins.

Score the outer edge of the letter slab (the face) and the corresponding face of the edge strip. Apply slip to both scored faces. Press the edge strip upright along the outer edge of the letter, working around curves by making small cuts on the inside of the strip to allow it to bend. Press firmly and blend the interior join with a wooden rib.

At corners (on letters like L, T, E, F), mitre the strip at 45 degrees for a neat join. Cut one piece to the corner point, then cut the next piece to the complementary angle and join them with score and slip.

Press a hanging loop into the back of the letter while the clay is still soft. Roll a clay rope 8 mm thick and 4 cm long. Bend it into a U shape and score-and-slip both ends to the back face of the letter slab in the upper third. Press firmly and smooth around the join points with a damp wooden rib.

Smooth the front face and outer edges of the letter with a damp sponge. Check the edge strip is flush with the front face of the letter. If the strip is slightly higher than the face, smooth it down with a wet finger.
Allow the letter to reach
leather-hard

. At this stage, cut any interior counter spaces with the fettling knife. Mark the cut lines with the needle tool first, then cut along the marked line, keeping the knife vertical. Remove the waste clay piece carefully. Smooth the interior edge of the counter with a damp sponge.

At leather-hard, press any decorative stamps or impressions into the face of the letter if desired. A repeating leaf stamp, a geometric border around the perimeter, or simple incised lines all work at this stage.
Drying
Cover loosely with plastic for the first 24 hours to slow drying to
leather-hard
. Remove the cover and allow to continue drying to
bone-dry

over three to five days. Dry the letter face-up on a flat surface. Do not prop it upright or hang it during drying: the weight of the edge strip on a soft slab can cause the letter to warp. A fully bone-dry letter is pale, lifts easily, and makes a faint hollow sound when tapped.
Finishing

Paint the bone-dry letter with acrylic paint before sealing. Apply a base coat over the front face and all edges; use a second colour on the face if you want a contrasting frame effect. Allow each coat to dry. Seal with two coats of matte or gloss varnish, allowing each coat to dry fully. Seal the back face and the hanging loop with at least one coat of diluted PVA to protect the clay body.
Care

Hang in a dry indoor location. Do not hang outdoors: air-dry clay is not weatherproof. Dust with a dry cloth. The hanging loop is load-rated for the weight of the letter only. Check the loop bond at the back of the letter once a year: re-bond with PVA if any movement is detected.
Variations

Make a set of three letters: initials of the household members or a short word. Keep the same font, scale, and colour scheme across all letters so they work together as a display. Space them evenly on the wall with equal gaps between each letter.

Press the letter face into a bed of salt before the clay stiffens to create a pitted, rough texture across the surface. Brush off the salt crystals at leather-hard: the small pocks left behind give the letter a stone or concrete appearance when painted in a grey or stone tone.

Embed small stones, pebbles, or glass beads into the face of the letter while the clay is soft, pressing each piece in with the wooden rib. Arrange them across the face as a mosaic before the clay stiffens. Seal once bone-dry with a thick coat of gloss varnish.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: Thin strokes on the letter break during drying
items.cause: The letter style had serifs or thin strokes that are too fragile in 7 mm slab clay
items.fix: At leather-hard, re-join the break with fresh slip. For the next attempt, use a bolder font with no strokes narrower than 10 mm

items.problem: Edge strip separates from the letter face
items.cause: The strip was attached when the slab face had already started to dry, weakening the score-and-slip bond
items.fix: At leather-hard, run the needle tool along the inside of the join to reopen it slightly, apply fresh slip, and press the strip back against the face. Support with a clay rope pressed into the inside corner

items.problem: Letter warps and leans to one side during drying
items.cause: The letter was dried upright before it was fully leather-hard, and the weight of the edge strip pulled the face slab out of shape
items.fix: Lay the letter face-up on a flat board and weight the corners with small tiles for 24 hours to coax it flat at leather-hard. Once bone-dry, a warp cannot be corrected without re-wetting

items.problem: Interior counter did not cut cleanly and edges are ragged
items.cause: The counter was cut when the clay was still too soft, causing the fettling knife to drag and squash the edge rather than cut cleanly
items.fix: Wait until full leather-hard before cutting counters. Use the needle tool to score the cut line first, then follow with the fettling knife in short, decisive strokes

items.problem: Hanging loop pulls away from the back under the weight of the letter
items.cause: The loop was bonded with a weak score-and-slip join or was attached when the back slab was already stiff
items.fix: Remove the loop, score deeply, apply generous slip, and re-attach. Back the loop with a small flat clay patch pressed over both loop ends and blended into the back face for added strength
